doc.title: Jason Palmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 2, 2025

title: Preparing students for a career: summer programs and royalties
summary: Palmer urges performance students to attend summer programs and meet peers, and teaches publishing and royalties.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: Do you get a sense of — as an educator — a responsibility to make your students aware of the employment opportunities these days — making a living in music. Do you talk about that? Like here’s what you need to know and here’s how you need to be?

Yeah. That comes up a lot you know, especially with students who, you know at Berklee they have a lot of different majors. You know you can major in music business, you can major in production, engineering, you know music therapy, whatever. But you know you also have performance majors who want to focus primarily on performance. So you know with those students we talk about what you need to do, how you need to be prepared, and also I try to show them, you know, this is a program that you should be going to in the summer. You know you should think about going to Siena, going to Jazz Ahead or going to Ravinia and meeting people who are serious and you know, forming those bonds. Because you know generationally those are going to be the players that you’re going to be playing with for the majority of your career. I mean that was my experience. And so you know I try to relate the experiences I’ve had, and also understand that you know my

experiences won’t necessarily be their experience but I just have to let them know okay this is what I went through and, you know, it’s a possibility for you as well. Another thing that I like to talk about a lot is royalties and having your music published and having it registered so you can really recoup the royalties that you’re entitled to even outside of just recording your music. Because I think a lot of students, they know that, okay if I put a record out then if it gets radio play or whatever, you know I’m entitled to royalties, but they don’t really understand that if you play your tunes at a gig then you’re also entitled to royalties because in this country a lot of those performance venues they have to pay a fee in order to have music at the venues. And so there are programs set up through BMI and ASCAP and all those — SECAC — that you know give royalties towards live performance. And so I always try to talk to them about those different kind of avenues of income possibilities. But yeah, it’s always a challenge for sure.
